drapeaux.note: Statement and interview fragments copied from the English Wikipedia page 'Rokeby Venus' (which cites The Times, March 11, 1914, and a 1952 interview); 'cruel wound in the neck' is quoted there from The Times.

titre: The Cleaver, the Suffragette, and the Venus at Her Mirror
accroche: In 1914, a militant slashes with a cleaver the only female nude Velázquez ever painted; almost forty years later, she adds another reason for her act.
contenu_vulgarise:
On March 10, 1914, Mary Richardson enters the National Gallery in London to attack Velázquez's Rokeby Venus (*Venus at Her Mirror*), the only female nude by Velázquez to have come down to us. According to Wikipedia, she attacks the canvas with a meat cleaver she smuggled into the museum. She leaves seven slashes, mostly between the figure's shoulders. The painting had been bought eight years earlier, in 1906, by the National Art Collections Fund for the National Gallery.

Richardson is a member of the Women's Social and Political Union (WSPU), the suffragist movement led by Emmeline Pankhurst. Soon afterward, she sends the WSPU a brief statement, which the press publishes: "I have tried to destroy the picture of the most beautiful woman in mythological history as a protest against the Government for destroying Mrs. Pankhurst, who is the most beautiful character in modern history." Wikipedia notes that her act was ostensibly provoked by the arrest of Emmeline Pankhurst the previous day, although there had already been warnings of a planned suffragette attack on the collection.

## A Militant Already Convicted

Richardson had already smashed windows at the Home Office and burned down, with her accomplice Jane Short, a historic mansion in Hampton, The Elms. Arrested nine times, she served prison terms totaling more than three years. She was also one of the first two women to be force-fed after the 1913 Cat and Mouse Act came into force. For the attack on the Venus, she is sentenced to six months in prison, the maximum allowed for destroying an artwork.

## A Canvas Read as a Body

The press of the day does not see the painting as mere artwork. Journalists describe the attack as a murder, nickname Richardson "Slasher Mary," and use words that evoke wounds inflicted on an actual female body: The Times describes a "cruel wound in the neck," as well as incisions to the shoulders and back. The scholar Lynda Nead writes that the incident came to represent a stereotypical image of feminism toward the female nude.

In 1952, according to Wikipedia, Richardson adds in an interview that she did not like "the way men visitors gaped at it all day long." The two explanations do not rule each other out: an immediate political protest, and unease at a man's gaze turned on a painted body. A word of caution: her biographer considers that none of the anecdotes in her 1953 autobiography is entirely true.

## What Remains

All the slashes were repaired by the National Gallery's chief restorer, Helmut Ruhemann, and the painting returned to the galleries. On November 6, 2023, two Just Stop Oil protesters broke the protective glass in front of it with hammers, demanding an end to new oil and gas licences in the UK.

repere.texte: Richardson leaves seven slashes on the canvas, mostly between the figure's shoulders; she is sentenced to six months in prison, the maximum allowed for destroying an artwork, and the painting is fully repaired by Helmut Ruhemann.

carte.punch: On March 10, 1914, a suffragette slashes with a cleaver the only female nude Velázquez painted.
carte.idee: Mary Richardson slashes Velázquez's Rokeby Venus seven times, an act ostensibly provoked by the arrest of Emmeline Pankhurst the day before. In 1952, she adds that she did not like the way men gaped at it.

quiz.question: Why does Mary Richardson target this particular painting on March 10, 1914?
choix: To protest the record price paid by the National Gallery to acquire it
To protest against the Government "destroying" Emmeline Pankhurst, arrested the day before
Because no woman painter was displayed in the same galleries of the museum
To prevent the sale of the painting to a collector living abroad
quiz.explication: In her statement to the WSPU, Richardson says she is protesting against the Government destroying Mrs. Pankhurst, arrested the day before according to Wikipedia; the purchase price, the absence of women painters, and a sale abroad are not among the reasons she gives at the time.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What weapon does Mary Richardson use to attack the painting, and how many blows does she land?
choix: A kitchen knife, for three quick blows
An ax hidden in a bag, for a single powerful blow
A hammer, for five blows on the painting's frame
A meat cleaver she smuggled into the museum, for seven blows
quiz_supplementaire.explication: According to Wikipedia, she attacks the canvas with a meat cleaver she smuggled into the museum, and leaves seven slashes.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What had Mary Richardson done before her attack on the Velázquez painting, according to the text?
choix: She had already vandalized another painting at the National Gallery
She had burned down, with Jane Short, the historic manor house of The Elms in Hampton
She had organized a demonstration in front of the British Parliament
She had been jailed for shoplifting
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Wikipedia says she had already burned down, with her accomplice Jane Short, the historic mansion of The Elms in Hampton.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What other reason does Mary Richardson give for her act, decades later, in 1952?
choix: She says she hated the gaze of the men who stood in front of the painting all day long
She says she wanted to protest the purchase price the museum paid for the painting
She says she acted on Emmeline Pankhurst's direct orders
She says she wanted to draw attention to her own work as a painter
quiz_supplementaire.explication: According to Wikipedia, Richardson adds in a 1952 interview that she did not like the way men visitors gaped at the painting all day long.
